question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}t,2t⟩$ at the point $t=\pi .$

The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡t$ and $y=2t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{t},2⟩ \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{t}+2{ln}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\pi $ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\pi ))] & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi }{\pi }+2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi  \\  & =2{ln}^{2}⁡\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

$$
∇f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}\,i+(x{e}^{xy}+2y)\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=t-1$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(t-1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}\,i+((t+1){e}^{(t+1)(t-1)}+2(t-1))\,j \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j \\  & =i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\,i+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}\cdot 1+((t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2)\cdot 1 \\  & =(t-1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+(t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2 \\  & =2t{e}^{{t}^{2}-1}+2t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(-1))] & =2(-1){e}^{(-1)^{2}-1}+2(-1)-2 \\  & =-2-2-2 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$

$$

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).

question.:question/problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $\mathbf{r}(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3⟩.\end{aligned}

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=\frac{1}{t},$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$

$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\cdot ⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩ \\  & =(-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 2t+(-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem:
The closed, positively oriented curve $C$ is defined as $\mathbf{r}(t)=10\operatorname{cos}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+10\operatorname{sin}t\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ).$ The outward-pointing unit normal vector on $C$ can be expressed as

$$
\mathbf{n}=\frac{a(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}+b(t)\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}}{||{\mathbf{r}}^{'}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $a(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
R=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-10\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{1}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}\begin{bmatrix}10\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+10\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=10\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨y{e}^{x+y}+xy{e}^{x+y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{x+y}+xy{e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨y(1+x){e}^{x+y}+2xy,\,x(1+y){e}^{x+y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,g(1,-1) & =⟨(-1)\cdot (1+1){e}^{1-1}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-1),\,1\cdot (1-1){e}^{1-1}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,1⟩\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/problem: Calculate the circulation $Γ$ of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=y\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{i}-x\hspace{0.167em}\mathbf{j}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ oriented counterclockwise.

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:

The gradient of the function $f(x,y,z)$ is defined as

$$
∇f(x,y,z)=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{i}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,\text{j}+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\,\text{k}.
$$

Since $∇f(x,y,z)=F(x,y,z),$ the function $f(x,y,z)$ must satisfy the following system:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x{y}^{3}z,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2},\,\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz
$$

First, we integrate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ with respect to $x.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $y$ and $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =\int \frac{∂f}{∂x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2x{y}^{3}z\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+g(y,z)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, differentiating the above expression with respect to $y,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y}
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂y}=3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}$ into account, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+\frac{∂g}{∂y} & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now we integrate $\frac{∂g}{∂y}$ with respect to $y.$ Note that the solution should contain an arbitrary function of $z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(y,z) & =\int \frac{∂g}{∂y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\int {z}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{z}^{2}+h(z)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $g(y,z)=y{z}^{2}+h(z)$ in the expression for $f(x,y,z),$ we get

$$
f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{y}^{3}z+y{z}^{2}+h(z).
$$

To determine the function $h(z),$ we differentiate $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z.$ This gives

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz+{h}^{′}(z).
$$

Taking $\frac{∂f}{∂z}={x}^{2}{y}^{3}+2yz$ into account, we obtain

$$

$$

where $C$ is a constant.

$$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem: Find the domain of the function $z=\frac{{x}^{3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function is well-defined at all points $(x,y)$ for which the following conditions are satisfied:

- The expression under the logarithm is positive, and

- the expression in the denominator is not equal to zero.

As a result, the points in the domain must satisfy the following inequalities: 

$$\begin{cases}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ \operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\ne 0\end{cases}\hspace{2em}⟹\hspace{2em}\begin{cases}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\end{cases}$$

Therefore, the domain is

$$\{(x,y)\in {\mathbb{R}}^{2}\hspace{0.167em}:\hspace{0.167em}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}>0,\hspace{0.222em}{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}\ne 1\}.$$

question.:question/problem:
Use Green's theorem to evaluate $$
{∮}_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r},
$$ where $\mathbf{F}(x,y)=⟨6{x}^{2}-xy+11,{y}^{2}+1⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,-1)$ and $(2,1).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](images/00/007634ca34871f05cde9d44a58fcf24b1e5fd3b8c337c68f2025fb8724eef819.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(6{x}^{2}-xy+11)\,dx+({y}^{2}+1)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=6{x}^{2}-xy+11$ and $Q(x,y)={y}^{2}+1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 2,-\frac{x}{2}\le y\le \frac{x}{2}\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(6{x}^{2}-xy+11)\,dx+({y}^{2}+1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[0-(-x)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-x/2}^{x/2}x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x[y]_{-x/2}^{x/2}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x(x)\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,dx \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
